opus-5.5.text:
I think the main driver is going to be the same thing that's driven most of the progress so far, which is scaling up compute. If you look at the history of the last decade or so, the amount of compute going into the largest training runs has grown by something like four to five times per year, and a lot of the capability gains we've seen can be traced back to that. I don't see a strong reason to expect that to stop over the next five years. There are physical and economic constraints, like power, chip production, and how much money investors are willing to put in, but those constraints still seem to leave a lot of room before they really bind.

That said, I don't think it's only going to be scaling pre-training in the naive way. Algorithmic progress has also been quite substantial. The estimates I find plausible suggest that the compute needed to reach a given level of performance has been falling by a factor of maybe three per year. So you get compounding gains from both hardware and software.

The other thing I'd emphasize is a shift in where that compute goes. We've already seen a move toward spending a lot more on post-training, reinforcement learning, and inference-time computation: letting models think longer, try multiple approaches, check their own work. I expect a lot of new capabilities, especially in agentic tasks, long-horizon planning, and doing real work on a computer, to come from training models in environments where they actually have to accomplish goals over extended periods, rather than just predicting text.

Where I'm more skeptical than some people is on how fast this translates into very general competence. Current systems are remarkably good at things that look impressive, like solving hard math problems or writing code for well-specified tasks, but they're still weaker at the things we take for granted in humans: coherent action over days or weeks, adapting to messy real-world contexts, and learning efficiently on the job. My guess is those capabilities will improve, but more gradually, and getting them right will require a lot more compute and better training environments rather than one clever insight. So I'd expect steady, impressive progress over five years, but not necessarily a sudden jump to systems that can automate most of the economy in that timeframe.

r001.rationale: The response discusses scaling compute and training methods, but does not say whether the transformer architecture will remain broadly stable.

r002.rationale: It expects capabilities to grow through more post-training and reinforcement learning, inference-time computation, and training in goal-oriented environments.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the honest answer is that the main driver is going to continue to be scale, in a fairly boring sense. If you look back at how capabilities have been acquired so far, most of it is not coming from clever new ideas. It's coming from people spending more compute on training, and the architecture, the data pipeline, the post-training methods all improving incrementally around that. I expect that to keep being the story for the next five years, because the compute scale-up is still ongoing. Frontier training runs are still growing at something like four or five times per year in effective compute, and the hardware and the capital to sustain that for at least a few more years seem to be there.

The second thing I'd point to is reinforcement learning on top of pretrained models. Pretraining gives you a model that has absorbed a huge amount of knowledge and some reasoning ability, but it's not very good at pursuing long tasks or correcting its own mistakes. What we've seen over the past couple of years is that if you take those models and train them with RL on verifiable tasks, like math and coding, you get big jumps in the ability to do multi-step work. I think the natural extension is that labs push this into domains where verification is harder, so you need better reward models, better environments, maybe real-world feedback. That's going to be where a lot of the interesting progress happens, and it's also where I'm most uncertain about how fast it goes, because it's not obvious how well the RL recipe transfers when you can't check answers cleanly.

Then the third piece is just the context around the model: longer context windows, tool use, memory, the ability to operate for hours or days on a task rather than minutes. A lot of what looks like a capability gain to a user is actually the model being able to act over longer horizons. And if you look at the metrics that try to measure this, the length of tasks models can complete has been doubling every several months, so I expect that trend to continue.

What I'd push back on is the idea that there's going to be some discrete moment where a new capability just appears. I think when people look closely at supposed emergent capabilities, they usually find smooth underlying trends with a threshold effect in the way we measure them. So my expectation is: no big surprises in the mechanism, continuous improvement that looks sudden only if you're measuring the wrong thing, and the biggest bottleneck being whether we can build training signals for the tasks we actually care about, which are the messy, long, hard-to-verify ones.

r001.rationale: The response presents scale as the main driver and describes architecture changes as incremental, implying the transformer architecture will remain broadly stable.

r002.rationale: It expects capability gains from training changes, especially reinforcement learning on pretrained models and improved training signals for harder tasks.

astra-6.text:
I think the main thing I’d expect is that we keep getting more capable systems as we scale up training, but increasingly also as we give systems more time to work on a problem after training. There’s a difference between asking a model to produce an answer immediately and letting it try several approaches, check its work, and use tools to gather feedback. You can get substantial improvements from that second approach even without changing the underlying architecture very much.

Another part of the story is training models on tasks where success is relatively easy to verify. With programming, for example, you can run the code and see whether it passes tests. That gives you a way to improve a system without having a human judge every answer. The harder question is how far those improvements transfer to situations where feedback is ambiguous or arrives much later.

I’d be cautious about predicting specific capabilities on a specific timeline. A model can become very impressive at individual tasks while still being unreliable over a long sequence of actions. If you want it to carry out a project that takes hours or days, small mistakes can accumulate, and recovering from those mistakes becomes a capability in its own right.

So over five years, I’d expect progress from a combination of larger training runs, better training methods, and more computation spent solving each problem. I don’t think we should assume transformers need to be replaced for that progress to happen. But how quickly it translates into systems that can autonomously do substantial portions of someone’s job is much more uncertain than whether benchmark performance will improve.

r001.rationale: The candidate says substantial gains can come without changing the architecture much and that transformers need not be replaced for progress to continue.

r002.rationale: The candidate expects capability gains from training on verifiable tasks and from better training methods.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the main way will be through scaling up training and giving systems more opportunities to learn from doing tasks. But I’d distinguish that from the claim that simply making a transformer bigger will automatically give us every capability we care about.

You can improve these systems along several dimensions: more computation during training, better data, better training objectives, and more computation when they’re actually solving a problem. A model that gives an immediate answer might fail at something that the same model can solve if it gets to try several approaches, use tools, and check its work. So some progress will come from how we use the models, as well as from improvements to the models themselves.

One particularly interesting possibility is a stronger feedback loop in domains where you can verify success. In programming, for example, a system can write code, run it, observe errors, and try again. If you can turn those interactions into useful training data, you have a way of improving capabilities that doesn’t depend entirely on finding more human-written text.

Over five years, I’d expect substantial progress, but I’m much less confident about the precise sequence of capabilities. Long tasks that require maintaining a coherent plan and recovering from mistakes seem like an important test. Getting better at individual steps doesn’t necessarily translate immediately into being reliable over hundreds of steps, and how quickly that gap closes matters a lot.

r001.rationale: The response discusses transformer systems but does not say whether their architecture will remain broadly stable.

r002.rationale: It expects capability gains from training changes, including more training compute, better data and objectives, and learning from task feedback.
